newsitem.title: UK: UK government jobs scheme gets cautious thumbs-up.
newsitem.headline: UK government jobs scheme gets cautious thumbs-up.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government will launch next week the most ambitious mass job creation scheme yet tried in this country and experts say it could yield real benefits.

A "welfare-to-work programme," funded by three to five billion pounds ($8.3 billion) from a windfall tax on Britain's privatised utilities, will be the centrepiece of Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's first budget on July 2.
That is an enormous sum of money -- far more than has ever been spent on job creation before. Importantly, it comes when most parts of the economy are flourishing and companies are looking to hire.

"Such a scheme is being introduced at the right time for the first time ever -- at the top of the business cycle," said Nick Isles, director of development at the Employment Policy Institute. "It's not a panic measure."
Brown plans to use the billions raised by the one-off tax to create work for 250,000 young people who have been unemployed for more than six months.

Employers will be offered a 60 pounds rebate each week for six months to take on a young, unemployed person under the age of 25. A rebate of 75 pounds per week will be offered to firms which take on someone out of work for more than two years.
Encouragingly, employers groups support the plan, although they think the windfall tax is unfair.
The Institute of Directors, in its budget submission, backed the plan but it said its aims were ambitious.
The Confederation of British Industry said: "The jobs subsidies proposed will be valuable for some businesses, especially smaller ones."
During the election campaign, Brown's predecessor, Kenneth Clarke, derided the scheme, saying a one-off windfall could never create jobs on an ongoing basis.
But experts said the sheer scale of the tax-take means anything is possible.

"It's an enormous amount of money, more than has ever been spent before," said Paul Johnson, deputy director at the Institute of Fiscal Studies. He said Britain now spends only about 500 million pounds on training each year.
"They could quite easily spend one to 1.5 billion for each of the next three or four years," he said, rather than blow the whole lot on a one-year programme.

But the scheme is by no means a guaranteed success. There is little to stop firms taking the rebate offered and employing young people for six months at the expense of others to whom they might otherwise have offered jobs.

Isles said it was therefore crucial to get Britain's major blue-chip companies involved in the scheme. This will be the job of Sir Peter Davies, chief executive of insurance giant Prudential Corp Plc and newly-appointed head of the Welfare-to-Work programme.

The more large companies that come on board, the less likely the scheme is to be abused. A 60 pound rebate to a company such as British Telecom, for example, on what would only be a tiny proportion of its huge workforce, is a pretty small sum.
But for a small company, the temptation to pocket the money and take advantage of cheap labour without offering valuable training would be much bigger.

"The danger is you just churn people through a series of low-paid, low-skilled jobs placements," Isles said. "But I am pretty certain there is the political will to do a lot better in terms of the jobs created.
"Nonetheless, policing this scheme will be very important and very costly. That's why the emphasis on big firms is important," he said.

Unless the unemployed are offered meaningful jobs that give them a chance to stay with a company beyond the rebate period, or at least to walk away with relevant experience to offer other employers, it will have failed.
Even if firms do not take advantage of the scheme to dip into a pool of cheap labour, Johnson said there was a risk of the young jobless getting work at the expense of older, unemployed counterparts.

"The fact that it might substitute for long-term unemployed over 25 is a worry. It seems plausible that the scheme will be extended to them at some point," said Johnson. That, of course, would be more expensive still.

Furthermore, the number of young, long-term unemployed has already shrunk to 180,000 from 250,000 since Labour announced the initiative, due to natural job creation in a growing economy, Isles said. Those that remain are a "hard core," some bordering on unemployable.
"Many of the client group are so disadvantaged, the work has to start well before you think about putting them into jobs," he said.

A case-managed approach, taking people before they get jobs, making them fit for work and seeing them through the whole process to permanent employment would be more expensive but pay greater dividends.

"The long-term unemployed are finding low-paid, low-skill work and cycling in and out of employment. They will be heavily represented in the government's target group and a six-month contract may not help them at all," Isles said.
Nonetheless, a well-directed plan, that will certainly be well funded, could create large numbers of jobs and large numbers of people who are more employable.
"It's a good time to be doing it while the economy is doing quite well and some firms are having trouble recruiting," Johnson said.
Official figures show claimant unemployment has fallen by about 500,000 over the last year, making it harder for companies gearing up to meet extra demand to find suitable employees.
But the benefit to the public finances may be small.

"The amount of the social security budget going to the long-term unemployed under the age of 25 is absolutely tiny," Johnson said. "You're talking only about one to two billion pounds out of a 100 billion pounds budget."
That is why parallel schemes to encourage single mothers into work are being considered and broader programmes must be looked at.

And if Britain's bubbling economy takes a turn for the worse, the costs of Labour's scheme will mushroom and success will be harder to come by. "If the economy slows down, it will become much tougher," Isles said. ($ = 0.604 British Pounds)
